[pap], reduplicated syllable imitating the flutter of wings.

pronunciation.approximation: 'eets-pah-PAHL-ohtl' — the name crackles like obsidian breaking; hold the second 'a' and the final 'o' long.

kin.label: Related beings
kin.form: Cihuateteo, the spirits of women who died in childbirth, of whom she is mother or queen.

kin.label: Astral role
kin.form: Tzitzimime, star-demons of the northern sky associated with eclipses.

pronunciation.note: The macrons on ā and ō mark reconstructed long vowels, making the restoration Tier 1. The name is onomatopoeic and lethal: a butterfly made of razor-sharp obsidian.

domains.title: Obsidian Butterfly
domains.subtitle: Stars, Tamoanchan, and the Cihuateteo
domains.lead: Itzpapālōtl is one of the most fearsome goddesses of the Nahua cosmos: a butterfly with wings of obsidian blades, mistress of Tamoanchan, and mother of the Cihuateteo. She is beauty that cuts, maternity that devours, and the star-demon who descends when the sun is darkened.

cards.name: Obsidian Wings
cards.desc: Her wings are edged with itztli, the black volcanic glass used for sacrifice and mirrors.

cards.name: Tamoanchan
cards.desc: The paradise of origins, where the gods created the first humans from ground bones.

cards.name: Mother of Cihuateteo
cards.desc: Women who died in childbirth became warrior spirits under her command, dangerous to the living.

cards.name: Eclipse Star
cards.desc: As a Tzitzimitl she leads star-demons against the sun, threatening cosmic collapse.

symbols.name: Obsidian butterfly
symbols.meaning: The union of delicate beauty and sacrificial cutting power.

symbols.name: Knife-edged wings
symbols.meaning: Instruments of war and childbirth, both forms of tearing that bring life or death.

symbols.name: Jaguar claws
symbols.meaning: Her taloned hands link her to the night hunters of the Mesoamerican forest.

symbols.name: Star headdress
symbols.meaning: Her identity as a Tzitzimitl, a stellar power that descends during eclipses.

mythology.lead: Itzpapālōtl belongs to the dangerous borderlands: between paradise and underworld, birth and death, daylight and eclipse. Her myths are preserved in fragments of the Florentine Codex, the Borgia-group codices, and late alphabetic histories — and where the evidence is late, the entry says so.

myths.title: The Lady of Tamoanchan
myths.text: Tamoanchan is the paradise of origins in Nahua thought — a lush mountain of flowers beyond the human world, where the gods dwelt and where humanity was fashioned (López Austin, Tamoanchan, Tlalocan). Itzpapālōtl rules there as guardian and terror at once: in the codices she appears with obsidian-bladed wings and taloned jaguar claws, mistress of a beauty that cuts the hand that touches it. The Florentine Codex treats her as one of the formidable powers of the upper world, and the name itself — ītztli, 'obsidian', joined to papālōtl, 'butterfly' (Karttunen, An Analytical Dictionary of Nahuatl) — is a theological statement: the loveliest thing in the air, built from the sharpest thing in the earth. In her, paradise and its danger are one flower.

myths.title: The Butterfly Who Led the Chichimecs
myths.text: Later alphabetic sources attach Itzpapālōtl to the Chichimec ancestors of the Mexica. The Historia de los Mexicanos por sus pinturas (c. 1540) names an obsidian butterfly among the wonder-beings of the migration age, and the Anales de Cuauhtitlan preserves the wider lore of the Chichimecs' star-guided wanderings out of Chicomoztoc, the Seven Caves. The evidence is late and fragmentary — friars wrote down what their informants said, and the Borgia-group codices show her sign without narrating her story — so the tradition should be cited with caution. But the association fits her astronomy: a people guided through the dark north by a star-demon. She is migration itself made divine — fragile as a butterfly, cutting as flint, leading the nameless toward an empire.

myths.title: Mother of the Cihuateteo
myths.text: Women who died in childbirth did not become ordinary dead. They became Cihuateteo, 'divine women' — fierce spirits who accompanied the sun from its zenith to the western horizon and descended at crossroads to threaten the living (Florentine Codex; Karttunen, s.v. cihuateotl). Itzpapālōtl is their mother and queen. The midwife's orations preserved in the Florentine Codex address the dead woman as a warrior fallen in battle, honoured like a slain captive: she had died, the texts say, capturing a child for the people. The theology is exact — childbirth was a war, the lying-in room a battlefield, and its queen a butterfly whose wings were blades. The myth dignifies a death no weapon caused, and reads maternity as the risk that wins.

myths.title: The Black Butterfly of Eclipse
myths.text: As a Tzitzimitl, Itzpapālōtl belongs to the star-demons of the northern sky — skeletal women, powers of the dark, who descend when the cosmic order fails (Seler's commentary on the Borgia group; Florentine Codex). During an eclipse the Nahua believed the Tzitzimime descended head-first to devour the sun or the moon, and the people answered with noise, raised weapons, and blood offerings until the light returned. Itzpapālōtl is the most terrible among them: the eclipse made personal, a black butterfly settling on the world's lamp. The rite is the meaning — chaos is fought not only with armies but with the gathered din of an entire people, terror communal answered communally, the way a whole village shouts at the dark until it lifts.

lore.syncretism: Colonial friars associated Itzpapālōtl with demons of the air and witches, flattening her complex identity into a Satanic figure. Modern scholars and artists have reclaimed her as an emblem of feminine ferocity, the dangerous side of motherhood, and the ecological violence of volcanic landscapes. Her image appears in Mexican feminist art and in celebrations of Día de los Muertos as a skeletal butterfly.
lore.culturalLegacy: Itzpapālōtl survives where Mesoamerican antiquity meets contemporary creativity. Her obsidian-butterfly form has inspired jewelry, tattoos, graphic novels, and installations that explore the beauty of the lethal. She is also a touchstone in studies of Nahua gender: the Cihuateteo show that childbirth was a battlefield as honoured as the warrior's, and that the dead women who fell in it were not victims but powers.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Itzpapālōtl refuses the categories that make goddesses safe. She is not a nurturing mother in the pastel sense; she is the mother whose children are weapons. She is not a gentle butterfly; she is a razor-winged eclipse. To encounter her is to understand that creation and destruction were never separate in Mesoamerican thought.

In her, the feminine is not domesticated. It is astronomical, surgical, and maternal all at once. She asks us to look at the things we call beautiful and ask what they cut. She asks us to look at the things we call monstrous and ask what they protect. The obsidian butterfly is still flying, and her wings still catch the light like broken glass.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is composed of ītztli ('obsidian') and papālōtl ('butterfly'). Classical Nahuatl used macrons to mark vowel length, now reconstructed from colonial sources and comparative Uto-Aztecan evidence. The final -tl is a single lateral affricate. There is no surviving pre-contact alphabetic text of the name; it is known from alphabetic Nahuatl manuscripts produced under Spanish supervision, above all the Florentine Codex.

lore.archaeology: No temple or inscription names Itzpapālōtl; her witnesses are the screenfold codices. Codex Borgia (c. 15th c., Puebla–Tlaxcala region) shows her repeatedly: a butterfly being with obsidian-tipped wings, taloned hands, and starry regalia, presiding over the ritual deer-hunt sequence and the Venus almanacs. Codex Laud and the Tonalamatl Aubin carry her day-sign associations, and the divinatory manuscripts give her sign, Tecpatl (flint), to births beneath her patronage. The Great Temple precinct itself yielded the physical vocabulary of her imagery: obsidian blades and mirrors by the tens of thousands in the Templo Mayor offerings, the sacrificial material her name fuses with the butterfly. Post-conquest alphabetic witnesses — Sahagún’s Florentine Codex (1570s) and the Historia de los Mexicanos — complete the record from indigenous informants.
